name: Quassia amara extract

lead: Quassia amara is a tropical shrub whose extract has been made into a 4% gel and tried on the face for rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis, aiming at less visible redness, flaking and a calmer-looking complexion.

Researchers cite its reported antiparasitic and anti-inflammatory properties. The human evidence is a 30-patient open-label rosacea study and a 60-patient randomized comparison in seborrheic dermatitis; other published work is in rats.

paras: In the studies it was applied to the affected facial skin as a gel over a treatment course. It is not a widely marketed product.
Tolerability findings are in the original reports; no wider safety or regulatory data were found.

angle.text: A 4% quassia gel has been tried on the face for rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis to reduce visible redness and flaking, using the plant's reported anti-inflammatory and antiparasitic properties. Two small studies have examined it.

lead: Quassia amara is a small evergreen shrub or tree of tropical Central and South America in the Simaroubaceae family, known for extreme bitterness from quassinoids such as quassin. Extracts of it are being studied in a 4 percent topical gel for two conditions that show on the face: rosacea, with its flushing, redness, papules and pustules, and facial seborrheic dermatitis, with its redness, scaling and itch.[1][2][3] People interested in calmer, clearer-looking facial skin may encounter it as a botanical alternative to the usual topical antifungals and antibiotics.

Both studies report that the gel was well tolerated: a 30-patient open-label rosacea study (27 completed) reported results the authors described as in line with topical metronidazole and azelaic acid, and a 60-patient randomised double-blind comparison in seborrheic dermatitis reported a significant efficacy advantage for the quassia gel over 2 percent ketoconazole and 1 percent ciclopirox olamine.[1][2] Other published work on the extract is in rats.[4][5]
No looksmaxxing-community discussion of this extract was found for this entry.
infobox: From Graman Quassi, a Surinamese healer; amara means bitter[3]
Bitter flavouring in beverages, organic insecticide[3]

paras: According to Wikipedia, Quassia amara grows in humid understory forests, has crimson flowers pollinated mainly by hummingbirds, and is cultivated for its wood, bark and roots. The genus is named for Graman Quassi, a Surinamese healer who introduced Europeans to its use against fever.[3]

Traditional uses include as a digestive tonic, fever remedy and parasite treatment, and research has explored antimalarial, antiulcer, blood-sugar-lowering and anti-leukemic effects, much of it preliminary. Its bitter extracts are used as an organic insecticide against aphids, beetles and some caterpillars, and the bark and wood flavour bitters such as Angostura and can substitute for hops in beer.[3]

The 4% gel has been investigated for rosacea of grades I to IV and for facial seborrheic dermatitis.[1][2] The studies' stated rationale was the antiparasitic and anti-inflammatory properties reported for the plant in rosacea, which is sometimes associated with Demodex mites, and its antifungal and anti-inflammatory properties in seborrheic dermatitis, which is associated with Malassezia yeasts.[1][2]

Rosacea. A single-center, open-label study enrolled 30 patients with rosacea grades I to IV and applied a 4% quassia extract gel for 6 weeks. Response was scored on flushing, erythema, telangiectasia, papules and pustules; 27 of 30 (90 percent) completed. The authors reported the treatment as very effective, with results in line with those published for topical metronidazole and azelaic acid, and described safety and tolerability as excellent.[1]

Seborrheic dermatitis. A randomised, double-blind study of 60 patients with facial seborrheic dermatitis assigned them to 4% quassia gel, 2% ketoconazole gel or 1% ciclopirox olamine gel for 4 weeks, with follow-up 4 weeks after treatment. Severity was scored 0 to 3 for erythema, scaling, pruritus and papules. Fifty-four (90 percent) completed; all three options were effective, with a significant advantage reported for the quassia extract and results for the other two in line with published literature.[2]
Both studies were small and from the same line of work, and neither has been reported with independent replication in the sources consulted.

In rats with nicotinamide-streptozotocin-induced diabetes, a standardized methanol extract (100 and 200 mg/kg for 14 days) reduced fasting blood glucose and improved glucose tolerance and lipid parameters.[4] Another rat study reported that the extract and the compound 2-methoxycanthin-6-one, but not quassin, inhibited indomethacin-induced gastric ulceration, with 77 to 85 percent cytoprotection at the higher doses and effects consistent with histamine H2 receptor involvement.[5] These are not studies of skin or appearance.

Both clinical reports describe tolerability as good.[1][2] Wikipedia notes that excessive use of the plant can cause vomiting and that animal studies suggest effects on fertility, so avoidance in pregnancy and long-term use is discouraged; these cautions concern the plant generally rather than the topical gel.[3]
